doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Joining Basie: names for the Chief, Sammy Davis and the first night
summary: Basie hires him personally; he plays with Sammy Davis at Harrah's, meets Freddie Green's stare and plays Wind Machine in Toledo.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Did he call himself Count? Do you recall?
I think he called himself Bill.

Yeah the guys called him a various assortment of names. Bill, Chief. I called him Chief. Some guys called him Count. Other guys called him Boss. It didn’t matter, he was just so well respected. He was a great guy. So I get the call from Count Basie. So he said, “Sonny Cohn, the manager, will be calling you shortly and he’ll let you know all the details.” He said, “we want you to join the band starting October 8.” And that was Labor Day. So that’s like six weeks. I was registered for school, all ready to go back to school. And actually I had just finished — it was amazing — my girlfriend at the time, who became my first wife and the mother of my children — we were sitting there watching the “Jerry Lewis Telathon.” And they just had Sammy Davis from Harrah’s in Lake Tahoe. I’m like oh man, wouldn’t it be great to get a gig like that. I swear five minutes later the phone rang and it was Basie on the phone. It was unbelievable. Two months after I joined the band we were sitting on the same stage at Harrah’s in Lake Tahoe with Sammy Davis. And every night I got to play three songs with Sammy, the Basie band would do about a half an hour warm-up. And then Sammy would come out and we’d do three songs. The first one was “My Shining Hour” I’ll never forget it. It was fast as hell and a lot of drum stuff in it. And I actually had Sammy Davis come up and say, “great job.” I remember Basie just looking up and smiling at me, because everything seems okay with the band. Freddie Green was kind of a grumbly old man but he didn’t ever say anything. Actually I used to get this from Freddie Green. See this arm moving, and then I’d see his arm stop and I knew what was coming he’d go like this. So as a young guy, 24 years old, Freddie Green started out kind of shaking his head and looking at you, I thought what am I doing wrong I thought it felt great. And then Cleveland Eaton the bass player would lean over and go, “don’t worry about him.” I’m like what, don’t worry about Freddie Green? Come on. So there was all this stuff going on. It was like wow,

what have I gotten myself into. After the first song we played the first night, I’ll never forget, Toledo, Ohio, Masonic Auditorium, 2000 people in the audience. And we played “Wind Machine” the first song. It was always the first opener. Sammy Nestico’s. Like a bat out of hell. And when we got to the end of that, the very first song I played with the band was “Wind Machine.” I was shaking so badly physically. I was behind the drums going I can’t believe this is it. Of course the next tune was a blues, and Basie starts out [scats and snaps fingers]. My hand was shaking so bad I couldn’t play those quarter notes I was talking about. Because you know, closed hi-hat. And hi-hat stand clicking. I couldn’t do it because my hand was going like this. And Cleve’s going, “settle down, relax.” I go, “I’m trying, I’m trying.” Eventually I kind of settled in. But you know, 24 years old and no rehearsal. My rehearsal was in the dressing room with Basie saying, “Is there anything I should know here? I’m only 24 years old why did I get this gig.” He says, “oh just kick ‘em in the ass. They haven’t had that in a while.”
